## Overview

`Tweedieverse` provides a unified differential analysis workflow for omics
measurements whose empirical variance structure is well represented by the
Tweedie family. The framework is intended for heterogeneous high-throughput
data, including microbiome abundances, single-cell RNA-seq measurements, bulk
RNA-seq summaries, metabolite intensities, and other continuous or count-like
assays.

The package uses Bioconductor containers as the primary interface. A single
omics assay is represented as a `SummarizedExperiment`,
`TreeSummarizedExperiment`, or `SingleCellExperiment`, and matched multi-omics
assays are represented as a `MultiAssayExperiment`. This keeps feature assays,
sample metadata, and experiment-level annotations together and makes the
workflow compatible with the broader Bioconductor ecosystem.

This vignette demonstrates six Bioconductor-oriented workflows:

- microbiome relative abundances stored in a `TreeSummarizedExperiment`,
- single-cell RNA-seq UMI counts stored in a `SingleCellExperiment`,
- single-cell RNA-seq non-UMI/read counts stored in a `SingleCellExperiment`,
- pseudobulk RNA-seq counts generated with `muscat::aggregateData()`,
- bulk RNA-seq counts from the Bioconductor `airway` dataset stored in a
    `SummarizedExperiment`,
- matched microbiome and metabolomics assays stored in a
    `MultiAssayExperiment`.

## Motivation

In omics data, biological processes or technical factors may induce distinct
statistical properties (such as overdispersion and zero-inflation) across
experimental platforms (or library preparation protocols). Most published
differential analysis methods are omics-specific and assume a single
probabilistic model for all features. `DESeq2` and `edgeR` use the negative
binomial distribution for sequencing counts. `MAST` uses a two-part hurdle
model for single-cell expression. `MaAsLin2` supports several microbiome
association models, including linear and compound Poisson models, while
`MaAsLin3` models prevalence and abundance separately. `limma` fits linear
models to expression data, including transformed RNA-seq measurements.

These choices ignore the fact that data distributions are feature-specific and
vary considerably both within and between platforms or technologies. A typical
multi-omics study therefore runs a different tool for each assay, each with its
own assumptions, preprocessing, and output format, and the resulting effect
sizes and significance calls are difficult to compare.

`Tweedieverse` provides a single home for differential analysis across omics
data types. It is built on Tweedie generalized linear models, whose flexibility
enables feature-specific modeling of omics data by adjusting a single
configuration parameter per feature: the Tweedie index `p`, which spans the
Gaussian, Poisson, compound Poisson-gamma, gamma, and inverse Gaussian
distributions.
`Tweedieverse` estimates `p` separately for each feature, so every feature is
modeled with a mean-variance relationship learned from its own data. This
yields a unified framework that adapts to biological and technological
variability in multi-omics profiles. Model adequacy and study design determine
the validity and power of the resulting tests; these examples demonstrate the
workflow rather than benchmark comparative performance.

With `Tweedieverse`, users can:

- run differential analysis on microbiome, single-cell, pseudobulk, bulk
    RNA-seq, and metabolomics data with one function, `Tweedieverse()`;
- pass data directly as a `SummarizedExperiment`, `SingleCellExperiment`,
    `TreeSummarizedExperiment`, or `MultiAssayExperiment`, with sample metadata
    and feature annotations kept intact;
- compare results across assays on a common scale, since every assay is
    analyzed with the same model family, testing procedure, and output format.

The sections below walk through each of these workflows.

## Relationship to existing tools

Bioconductor provides established differential-analysis workflows:
[DESeq2](https://bioconductor.org/packages/DESeq2) and
[edgeR](https://bioconductor.org/packages/edgeR) use negative-binomial models
for
sequencing counts; [limma](https://bioconductor.org/packages/limma) uses linear
models with empirical Bayes inference, including precision-weighted RNA-seq
analysis with voom. [MAST](https://bioconductor.org/packages/MAST) uses a
two-part
hurdle model for single-cell detection and positive expression.
[MaAsLin2](https://bioconductor.org/packages/Maaslin2) offers multivariable
meta-omic association analysis with several model choices, including compound
Poisson models, while
[MaAsLin3](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/maaslin3.html)
combines prevalence and abundance analyses.

Tweedie modeling is also available through general-purpose CRAN tools.
[cplm](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=cplm) fits compound Poisson regression
models, and [glmmTMB](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=glmmTMB) supports
Tweedie
generalized linear mixed models.
[statmod](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=statmod) supplies Tweedie GLM
families, while [tweedie](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=tweedie) provides
distribution and likelihood calculations. Tweedieverse uses cplm, glmmTMB, and
statmod as modeling engines.

Tweedieverse adds a common omics workflow around these engines: direct
Bioconductor-container input, sample alignment, feature filtering,
domain-specific size-factor offsets, feature-wise fitting, optional prevalence
tests, multiple-testing correction, and consistently structured association
tables. It supports both fixed and estimated variance powers and analyzes
`MultiAssayExperiment` layers through the same interface. Each layer is fitted
independently; effect sizes retain their assay- and link-specific
interpretation.

## Installation

After Bioconductor acceptance, the release version can be installed with:

```{r install-bioc, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("Tweedieverse")
```

The development version can be installed from GitHub:

```{r install-github, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("remotes")
}

remotes::install_github("himelmallick/Tweedieverse")
```

```{r packages}
library(Tweedieverse)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(TreeSummarizedExperiment)
library(MultiAssayExperiment)
library(muscat)
library(airway)
```

## Loading Packaged Example Data

The example containers used in this vignette are distributed with the package
under `inst/extdata`. This allows the vignette to run during Bioconductor
checks without network access.

The microbiome and UMI examples are compact subsets of the real HMP2 and
PBMC3k datasets used in the original
[TweedieLabs tutorials](https://github.com/himelmallick/TweedieLabs).
The non-UMI example uses CC BY 4.0 Tabula Muris Smart-seq2 brain data.
The Franzosa multi-omics example comes from the
[HuMMANet v1 archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22053943).
The preparation code, source details, and per-object licences are included in
scripts/rebuild_example_data.R, scripts/README.md, and
extdata/DATA_LICENSES.md inside the installed package.

```{r load-example-data}
microbiome_tse <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "microbiome_tse.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
umi_sce <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "umi_sce.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
nonumi_sce <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "nonumi_sce.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
franzosa_example_mae <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "franzosa_example_mae.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
```

## Microbiome Relative Abundance Example

For microbiome data, `Tweedieverse()` accepts a
`TreeSummarizedExperiment`. The assay contains taxa/features in rows and
samples in columns; `colData` contains sample metadata.

This subset contains the 20 most variable taxa across 48 baseline HMP2 samples,
with 16 samples each from the nonIBD, CD, and UC groups. The source tables are
distributed with MaAsLin2. Baseline selection and metadata preparation follow
the
[original microbiome tutorial](https://github.com/himelmallick/TweedieLabs)
.

The example table contains relative abundances, so this analysis disables
additional offset normalization by setting `normalization = "NONE"`. For raw
microbiome counts, omit that argument to use the microbiome default `TSS`
size-factor offset.

```{r microbiome-fit}
microbiome_tse

microbiome_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = microbiome_tse,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "microbiome",
    normalization = "NONE",
    fixed_effects = c("diagnosis", "antibiotics", "age"),
    reference = "diagnosis,nonIBD",
    return_all = TRUE,
    tweedie_p = NULL,
    median_comparison = FALSE
)

head(microbiome_fit)
```

### Reading the result table

Each row describes one feature--covariate coefficient. Factor variables can
produce several rows per feature, one per non-reference level. These examples
use `median_comparison = FALSE` and the default log link.

- `feature` , `metadata` , `value` : Feature identifier, tested covariate, and
    factor level or continuous predictor name. Factor effects are relative to
    the reference level.
- `coef` , `stderr` : Estimated coefficient and its standard error on the link
    scale. With a log link, `exp(coef)` is the fitted mean ratio at equal
    offsets. Continuous covariates are standardized by default, so their
    coefficients describe a one-standard-deviation increase unless
    `standardize = FALSE` .
- `pval` , `qval` : Unadjusted test p-value and multiple-testing adjusted
    p-value (Benjamini--Hochberg by default across the reported coefficient
    tests within an assay).
- `base.model` , `tweedie.index` : Model engine/family label and estimated or
    fixed variance power.
- `N` , `N.not.zero` , `percent.zero` : Aligned sample count, number with
    positive measurements, and rounded percentage of observed measurements equal
    to zero. Missing model covariates can reduce a particular fit's effective
    sample count.

`return_all = TRUE` keeps the full result table in memory. The default returns
only rows with `qval <= max_significance` (default 0.05). An empty default table
means no returned associations meet that cutoff, rather than no models were
attempted. Failed fits produce feature-named warnings and are absent from the
result table; inspect those warnings before interpreting the results.
The number of hypotheses here covers only the selected features;
these q-values are not results from testing the entire source dataset.

```{r microbiome-interpretation}
diagnosis_results <- subset(microbiome_fit, metadata == "diagnosis")
diagnosis_results$mean_ratio <- exp(diagnosis_results$coef)
head(diagnosis_results[, c(
    "feature", "value", "coef", "mean_ratio", "pval", "qval"
)], 2)
```

The first displayed diagnosis association is
**`r diagnosis_results$feature[1]`** in **`r diagnosis_results$value[1]`**
relative to nonIBD: its coefficient is
`r round(diagnosis_results$coef[1], 2)` and its adjusted p-value is
`r signif(diagnosis_results$qval[1], 3)`.
The second is **`r diagnosis_results$feature[2]`**, with coefficient
`r round(diagnosis_results$coef[2], 2)` and adjusted p-value
`r signif(diagnosis_results$qval[2], 3)`.
A positive coefficient indicates higher fitted relative abundance and a negative
coefficient lower fitted relative abundance, adjusting for age and antibiotic
use. These are conditional associations in this subset, not evidence of
causality.

### Visualizing associations

For an exploratory overview, the heatmap below includes associations meeting
`qval <= 0.25`, an explicitly relaxed 25% FDR threshold. It shows up to five
features and all retained contrasts for those features. The package heatmap
uses signed `-log(qval)`, clipped to [-20, 20]: red denotes positive abundance
coefficients and blue negative coefficients. Larger magnitudes indicate
stronger evidence. Empty feature--contrast combinations are displayed as zero;
they do not establish absence of an effect. The plot's significance label refers
to the chosen 0.25 cutoff.

```{r microbiome-heatmap, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=1.8, out.width="100%"}
heatmap_results <- subset(microbiome_fit, !is.na(qval) & qval <= 0.25)
Tweedieverse_heatmap(
    output_results = heatmap_results,
    cell_value = "qval",
    first_n = 5,
    title = "HMP2 associations (q <= 0.25)",
    data_label = "Taxon",
    metadata_label = "Covariate / contrast"
)
```

## Single-Cell RNA-seq UMI Count Example

For single-cell RNA-seq data, `Tweedieverse()` accepts a
`SingleCellExperiment`. The UMI example uses integer molecule counts.

This subset contains 20 genes and 60 PBMC3k cells, with 30 CD4 and 30 CD8 cells.
Cell labels and raw UMI counts come from the processed object used in the
[original UMI tutorial](https://github.com/himelmallick/TweedieLabs)
.
Genes are selected by count variance across the retained cells.

UMI counts are count-like. Here we pin the variance power to `p = 1`, the
Poisson variance case, and use the single-cell domain. The library sizes in
colData were calculated using all source genes before selecting the 20 genes.
Passing `scale_factor = "library_size"` uses those full-library sizes as
offsets.

```{r umi-fit}
umi_sce

umi_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = umi_sce,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "single_cell",
    scale_factor = "library_size",
    fixed_effects = "CellType",
    reference = "CellType,CD8",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE
)

head(umi_fit)
```

The `CellType` rows compare CD4 with the CD8 reference group. For example,
**`r umi_fit$feature[1]`** has coefficient `r round(umi_fit$coef[1], 2)`
and q-value `r signif(umi_fit$qval[1], 3)`. At equal library size, its fitted
CD4/CD8 mean ratio is `r round(exp(umi_fit$coef[1]), 2)`.
This is a cell-type illustration from one donor. Cells are not independent
biological replicates for population-level treatment inference; use replicated
samples and an appropriate design for that question.


## Single-Cell RNA-seq Non-UMI / Read Count Example

The non-UMI example uses read-count-like measurements. These can have a more
flexible mean-variance relationship than UMI counts, so we leave
`tweedie_p = NULL` and let Tweedieverse estimate the index after filtering.

The source is the original Tabula Muris Smart-seq2 FACS dataset, distributed
under CC BY 4.0 in
[Figshare version 8](https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.5829687.v8).
This example retains 20 genes and 60 cells from mouse 3_10_M, balanced between
astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. The SCRAN factors in colData were computed on
all source genes for these cells before selecting the 20 most variable genes.
The source counts are unchanged. This is a cell-type illustration within one
mouse; it does not establish population-level differential expression across
biological replicates. See the
[original study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0590-4).

```{r nonumi-fit}
nonumi_sce

nonumi_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = nonumi_sce,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "single_cell",
    scale_factor = "source_size_factor",
    fixed_effects = "celltype",
    reference = "celltype,astrocyte",
    standardize = FALSE,
    tweedie_p = NULL,
    median_comparison = FALSE
)

head(nonumi_fit)
```

Here the contrast is oligodendrocytes relative to astrocytes. The first returned
gene, **`r nonumi_fit$feature[1]`**, has coefficient
`r round(nonumi_fit$coef[1], 2)`, q-value `r signif(nonumi_fit$qval[1], 3)`,
and fitted variance power `r nonumi_fit$tweedie.index[1]`.
The coefficient's sign describes the direction after accounting for the
precomputed SCRAN factor. The fitted index describes the variance model; it
is not an effect size or significance measure.


## Pseudobulk Single-Cell RNA-seq Example

Pseudobulk analysis aggregates single-cell counts to sample-level counts before
modeling. This is useful when the biological replicate, rather than the cell,
is the experimental unit. The `muscat` package provides a Bioconductor-native
workflow for this aggregation. Its `aggregateData()` function summarizes a
`SingleCellExperiment` by variables in `colData`, commonly
`cluster_id` and `sample_id`.

This example follows the workflow used by the `muscat` vignette:
multi-subject single-cell data are first represented as a prepared
`SingleCellExperiment`, cells are aggregated into cluster-by-sample pseudobulk
counts, and the resulting sample-level count matrix is analyzed with
`Tweedieverse()`. The package-provided `example_sce` object contains the
required `cluster_id`, `sample_id`, and `group_id` fields and is a lightweight
version of the Kang et al. interferon stimulation example used throughout
`muscat`.

```{r pseudobulk-fit}
data("example_sce", package = "muscat")

pseudobulk_input <- example_sce[seq_len(100), ]

pseudobulk_sce <- muscat::aggregateData(
    pseudobulk_input,
    assay = "counts",
    fun = "sum",
    by = c("cluster_id", "sample_id"),
    verbose = FALSE
)

SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(pseudobulk_sce)

pseudobulk_assay <- "CD4 T cells"
pseudobulk_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(
    pseudobulk_sce,
    pseudobulk_assay
)
top_pseudobulk_genes <- order(
    rowSums(pseudobulk_counts),
    decreasing = TRUE
)[seq_len(20)]

pseudobulk_metadata <- unique(as.data.frame(
    SummarizedExperiment::colData(pseudobulk_input)[, c("sample_id",
        "group_id")]
))
rownames(pseudobulk_metadata) <- pseudobulk_metadata$sample_id
pseudobulk_metadata <- pseudobulk_metadata[
    colnames(pseudobulk_counts), ,
    drop = FALSE
]
pseudobulk_metadata$condition <- pseudobulk_metadata$group_id

pseudobulk_se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = pseudobulk_counts[top_pseudobulk_genes, , drop =
        FALSE]),
    colData = pseudobulk_metadata
)

pseudobulk_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = pseudobulk_se,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "bulk_rnaseq",
    fixed_effects = c("condition"),
    reference = "condition,ctrl",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    max_significance = 1
)

head(pseudobulk_fit)
```

The `condition` coefficient compares stimulated samples with control samples
within CD4 T cells. For **`r pseudobulk_fit$feature[1]`**, the coefficient is
`r round(pseudobulk_fit$coef[1], 2)` and q-value is
`r signif(pseudobulk_fit$qval[1], 3)`. The rows represent sample-level
pseudobulks rather than individual cells, so `N` counts pseudobulk samples.
`max_significance = 1` displays all available tests, including weak evidence;
it does not declare them all significant. This compact example omits donor
blocking; a paired stimulation study should include donor in the model.


## Bulk RNA-seq Count Example

For bulk RNA-seq data, `Tweedieverse()` accepts a `SummarizedExperiment`.
This example uses the Bioconductor `airway` dataset, which contains RNA-seq
read counts from airway smooth muscle cells treated with dexamethasone.

The full `airway` object contains tens of thousands of genes. To keep the
vignette fast, the example keeps a small set of high-count genes while
preserving the original `airway` sample metadata. Bulk RNA-seq uses `TMM` as
the default normalization strategy in `Tweedieverse`; this computes
library-size factors for the model offset without modifying the count assay.

Set `run_presence_absence_model = TRUE` to include a test for whether the
feature is detected. By default, the prevalence fit requires at least three
samples with nonzero counts and three with zero counts for each gene.
Use `min_presence_absence_count` to change both minimums. In bulk and pseudobulk
data, genes with only one or two zeros can still enter the abundance analysis.
For retained genes below either minimum, `pval_presence` is `NA` and
`pval_abundance` becomes the joint `pval`. When the two
reported p-values are exactly 0 and 1, the joint `pval` is 0. Tweedieverse
applies the selected multiple-testing correction to the joint p-values to
compute `qval`.

Use `return_all = TRUE` to retrieve the full association table with
`output = NULL`, including associations above `max_significance`.
The default returns associations passing the threshold. Missing q-values after
median comparison are retained in the full table and excluded from significant
results.

```{r bulk-rnaseq-fit}
data("airway", package = "airway")

airway_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(airway, "counts")
top_airway_genes <- order(rowSums(airway_counts), decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(
    20)]

bulk_rnaseq_se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = airway_counts[top_airway_genes, , drop = FALSE]),
    colData = SummarizedExperiment::colData(airway)
)

bulk_rnaseq_se

bulk_rnaseq_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = bulk_rnaseq_se,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "bulk_rnaseq",
    fixed_effects = c("dex"),
    reference = "dex,untrt",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    run_presence_absence_model = TRUE,
    max_significance = 0.05,
    return_all = TRUE
)

head(bulk_rnaseq_fit)
```

The `dex` contrast compares dexamethasone-treated with untreated samples.
For **`r bulk_rnaseq_fit$feature[1]`**, `coef_abundance` is
`r round(bulk_rnaseq_fit$coef_abundance[1], 2)` and the joint q-value is
`r signif(bulk_rnaseq_fit$qval[1], 3)`. A positive abundance coefficient
indicates higher offset-adjusted mean counts in treated samples.

With the presence model enabled, `coef` and `stderr` retain abundance-model
meaning; the joint CCT p-value is not a test of a combined effect size.
`coef_presence` is a logistic-model log-odds coefficient, while
`pval_abundance`/`qval_abundance` and `pval_presence`/`qval_presence` describe
component tests. Inspect `pval_presence` to see which genes lacked enough zeros
or detections to fit the prevalence model. For those genes, the joint p-value
falls back to the abundance p-value. `return_all = TRUE` includes rows above
0.05; use `subset(bulk_rnaseq_fit, !is.na(qval) & qval <= 0.05)` for discovery
selection. The full airway experiment is paired by cell line; include `cell`
alongside `dex` when analyzing that study design.


## Multi-omics Container

For multi-omics data, `Tweedieverse()` accepts a `MultiAssayExperiment`.
The packaged Franzosa et al. example is stored as an individual `.rds` file in
`inst/extdata`. It contains matched microbiome species abundances and
metabolite profiles. Each omics layer is analyzed independently, and per-omics
parameters can be supplied as named vectors or lists.

```{r multiassay}
franzosa_example_mae

multi_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = franzosa_example_mae,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "abundance",
    domain = c(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = "microbiome",
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = "custom"
    ),
    normalization = c(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = "NONE",
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = "MEDIAN"
    ),
    fixed_effects = c("diseaseCat_clean", "Age"),
    tweedie_p = list(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = NULL,
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = NULL
    ),
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    max_significance = 1
)

names(multi_fit)
head(multi_fit$taxaAbundanceProfile)
head(multi_fit$harmonizedMetaboliteProfile)
```

Each list element is a separate association table, and its `omics` column
identifies the layer. `diseaseCat_clean` rows compare the named `value` with the
reference disease category; `Age` rows describe a one-standard-deviation
increase
because continuous predictors are standardized by default. Within either layer,
a positive log-link coefficient means a higher fitted mean, conditional on the
other covariate and offset. Taxon abundances and metabolite intensities have
different measurement scales, so coefficients should be interpreted within
layers. q-values are adjusted separately per layer, not across the entire
multi-omics list. As above, `max_significance = 1` displays tests without
requiring
a discovery threshold.


Median comparison uses Monte Carlo simulations when `median_comparison = TRUE`.
Set `median_comparison_seed = 123` to reproduce those simulations.
The seed is scoped with `withr`, restoring the preceding random-number state
after the median-comparison calculation. When the seed is `NULL`, results can
vary between runs.

## Session Info

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
